title: 1 Chronicles 8:29–40
context: This unit traces a Benjamite family living at Gibeon and in Jerusalem, and through it the line of Saul, continued for many generations through Jonathan. The same genealogy appears again, with small differences, in 9:35–44, where it leads directly into the account of Saul’s death in chapter 10. The Chronicler does not explain why the list is given twice, and suggested reasons are inferences. 8:33 makes Ner the father of Kish, while 1 Samuel 9:1 calls Kish “the son of Abiel” and 1 Samuel 14:51 calls Ner “the son of Abiel”; the texts do not explain the relationship. The names Eshbaal and Merib-baal (8:33–34) are often identified with the Ishbosheth of 2 Samuel 2:8 and the Mephibosheth of 2 Samuel 4:4, whose son is called Mica in 2 Samuel 9:12, but Chronicles does not state the identification, and this page holds it as probable rather than certain. 1 Samuel 14:49 lists Saul’s sons as Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua, a different list from 8:33. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: even after Saul’s fall, his descendants through Jonathan continued among the people of Benjamin.

verses.text: The father of Gibeon, whose wife’s name was Maacah, lived in Gibeon
verses.arminianNotes: The father of Gibeon, whose wife was Maacah, lived in Gibeon. Arminian readers note that this family introduces Saul’s ancestry by way of a Benjamite town. The repeated list in 9:35 names him Jeiel, a detail recorded plainly without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the Gibeon setting and the parallel in 9:35. Gibeon would later be an important place of worship (16:39). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the start of a family record that leads to Saul, and neither draws doctrinal conclusions from the setting.

verses.text: with his firstborn son Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab,
verses.arminianNotes: The firstborn Abdon and his brothers Zur, Kish, Baal, and Nadab are named. Arminian readers note that the parallel list in 9:36 also names Ner here. They accept the difference as part of the honest transmission of these records, without forcing agreement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the difference from 9:36 and do not resolve it by speculation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the family record of Gibeon and affirm the reliability of Scripture without requiring every parallel list to match exactly.

verses.arminianNotes: Gedor, Ahio, and Zecher continue the list of brothers. Arminian readers note that the parallel in 9:37 reads Zechariah, a variation in the form of the name. Such differences are common in ancient lists and do not affect the family’s identity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the variant form calmly. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and agree that spelling differences between parallel lists raise no doctrinal issue, while honoring the families the list preserves.

verses.text: and Mikloth, who became the father of Shimeah. They also lived with their families in Jerusalem, near their relatives.
verses.arminianNotes: Mikloth fathers Shimeah, and the family lives in Jerusalem near their relatives. Arminian readers note that a Gibeonite family also had a presence in Jerusalem. The record shows Benjamin’s ties to the city that would become the center of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the family’s place in Jerusalem and the parallel in 9:38, which reads Shimeam. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as connecting Saul’s wider family with Jerusalem, a reminder that Benjamin remained part of the community gathered around God’s house.

verses.text: Ner became the father of Kish. Kish became the father of Saul. Saul became the father of Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal.
verses.arminianNotes: Ner fathers Kish, Kish fathers Saul, and Saul’s sons are Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal. Arminian readers note that 1 Samuel 9:1 calls Kish “the son of Abiel” and 1 Samuel 14:49 gives a different list of sons; the texts do not explain the relationship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the different lists without forcing a harmony. Eshbaal is often identified with Ishbosheth (2 Samuel 2:8), though Chronicles does not say so. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Saul’s genealogy and caution against speculation about the differences.

verses.text: The son of Jonathan was Merib-baal. Merib-baal became the father of Micah.
verses.arminianNotes: Jonathan’s son is Merib-baal, the father of Micah. Arminian readers note that Merib-baal is often identified with Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 4:4), whose son is called Mica in 2 Samuel 9:12. They hold the identification as probable, since Chronicles does not state it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the identification as likely but unstated. If it holds, the line recalls David’s kindness to Jonathan’s son for Jonathan’s sake. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as continuing Jonathan’s line and see in it the survival of a family remembered with covenant kindness.

verses.text: The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz.
verses.arminianNotes: Micah’s sons are Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz. Arminian readers note that the line continues several generations after Saul. The parallel in 9:41 reads Tahrea, a minor variation. The family of Jonathan endured long after the fall of Saul’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the continuation of the line and the minor variation in spelling. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as evidence that Saul’s descendants through Jonathan continued among the people of Benjamin, and neither builds doctrine on the names.

verses.text: Ahaz became the father of Jehoaddah. Jehoaddah became the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Zimri became the father of Moza.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz fathers Jehoaddah, whose sons include Zimri, the father of Moza. Arminian readers note that the parallel in 9:42 reads Jarah for Jehoaddah. They record the difference plainly and read the verse as a continuing family record.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the variant and do not force agreement. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and affirm that the faithful preservation of these lists does not depend on harmonizing every form of a name.

verses.text: Moza became the father of Binea. Raphah was his son, Eleasah his son, and Azel his son.
verses.arminianNotes: Moza fathers Binea, followed by Raphah, Eleasah, and Azel. Arminian readers note the father-to-son pattern that carries Jonathan’s line forward. The parallel in 9:43 reads Rephaiah for Raphah, another minor variation in the record.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the continuity and the variant form. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a link in the chain of generations and see in it the long survival of Saul’s family through Jonathan, recorded without comment.

verses.text: Azel had six sons, whose names are these: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel.
verses.arminianNotes: Azel has six sons: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. Arminian readers note the full list of names, which shows a flourishing family. Generations after Saul, Jonathan’s descendants remained a recognized household in Benjamin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a flourishing line and note that the same six names appear in 9:44. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as continuing the family record and see God’s preservation of Jonathan’s descendants, without assigning a reason the text does not give.

verses.text: The sons of Eshek his brother: Ulam his firstborn, Jeush the second, and Eliphelet the third.
verses.arminianNotes: The sons of Eshek, Azel’s brother, are Ulam, Jeush, and Eliphelet. Arminian readers note that this branch is not repeated in chapter 9. The extra material shows that chapter 8 gives the fuller version of the family record.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that 9:35–44 stops before this verse. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail and agree that the difference in length between the two lists is recorded plainly, without an explanation the text does not supply.

verses.text: The sons of Ulam were mighty men of valor, archers, and had many sons, and grandsons, one hundred fifty. All these were of the sons of Benjamin.
verses.arminianNotes: Ulam’s sons are mighty men of valor and archers, with many sons and grandsons, 150 in all. Arminian readers note the closing tribute to a vigorous family. Benjamite archers are remembered elsewhere in Chronicles (12:2), and this line carried on that skill.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the flourishing family a sign of God’s blessing on Jonathan’s descendants long after Saul. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an honorable close to Benjamin’s record and see in it God’s continued care for the tribe of Saul.
